description: Catalog of test methodologies and programming patterns used to map a project's projectPatterns to projectCapabilities and to steer LLM code generation. Every pattern belongs to exactly one category; categories describe how patterns may be combined and which are mutually exclusive. Each pattern carries a description, when-to-use guidance, and concrete rules an LLM must follow when the pattern is enabled.

usage.selection: Categories with selection 'single' allow at most one pattern; 'multiple' allows any compatible subset. 'mutuallyExclusive' means patterns in the category cannot be combined. Cross-category conflicts are listed per pattern in conflictsWith.
usage.generation: Only generate code for enabled patterns. If a requested pattern conflicts with an enabled one, surface the conflict and ask the user to resolve it instead of silently choosing.
usage.rule_precedence: A pattern's rules are constraints, not suggestions. If a rule cannot be satisfied, report why rather than violating it.

categories.name: Test methodology
categories.description: How tests drive the development workflow. Choose at most one.
guidance: TDD is best for developers who want to build clean, testable code incrementally.
BDD is ideal when you need strong collaboration between technical and non-technical teams.
ATDD is useful when aligning development with clear business acceptance criteria.
SDD is good for projects where plain-language specs are a key part of the process.

categories.name: Object creation
categories.description: How objects are constructed and managed. Most projects use a Factory; add a Builder, Prototype, Singleton, or Object Pool only when the design calls for it.

categories.name: State and behaviour
categories.description: How an object's behaviour is structured and varied. State Machine and Strategy can coexist when modes and algorithms vary independently.

categories.name: Communication
categories.description: How components notify and interact with each other. Prefer a single primary notification style: a local Observer or a global Event Bus, not both.

categories.name: Dependency resolution
categories.description: How components obtain their dependencies. Choose Dependency Injection or Service Locator, not both.

categories.name: Structure
categories.description: Structural patterns that shape how objects are composed and accessed. These generally compose freely.

categories.name: Application architecture
categories.description: Top-level separation of concerns. ECS and the view-model architectures (MVC/MVP/MVVM) are competing paradigms; choose one.

categories.name: Persistence
categories.description: How domain state is read from and written to storage. Repository and Unit of Work are designed to work together.

categories.name: Concurrency
categories.description: How concurrent work is coordinated. These patterns compose.

patterns.name: Test-Driven Development (TDD / FTF)
patterns.description: Drive design with a failing test first: write a test that captures the next behaviour, make it pass with the minimum production code, then refactor. FTF (Failing Test First) is the red step of the cycle.
patterns.whenToUse: Incremental work on logic-heavy code with clear inputs and outputs, when clean testable code and fast feedback are priorities.
rules: Never write production code without a failing test that requires it.
Cycle red -> green -> refactor in small steps; keep the code compiling at each step.
Confirm the new test fails for the expected reason before implementing.
Test behaviour through public contracts, not private implementation details.
Keep tests fast, deterministic, and independent of execution order.

patterns.name: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)
patterns.description: Specify behaviour as shared Given/When/Then scenarios that technical and non-technical stakeholders can both read.
patterns.whenToUse: When collaboration between developers, QA, and business stakeholders matters and requirements are best expressed as examples.
rules: Express each scenario as Given (context), When (action), Then (observable outcome).
Write scenarios in the project's ubiquitous language; avoid implementation detail.
Automate scenarios so they run as executable acceptance tests.
Keep one behaviour per scenario; avoid chained When/Then sequences.

patterns.name: Acceptance-Test-Driven Development (ATDD)
patterns.description: Derive implementation from acceptance criteria agreed with the customer before coding; the acceptance test defines done.
patterns.whenToUse: When clear business acceptance criteria exist and development must align to them.
rules: Agree the acceptance criteria and a failing acceptance test before implementation.
Treat the acceptance test as the definition of done for the feature.
Use unit-level TDD inside the acceptance test where useful.
Keep acceptance tests at the user-visible boundary.

patterns.name: Specification-Driven Development (SDD)
patterns.description: Write a precise, plain-language specification first and guide or generate the implementation from it.
patterns.whenToUse: When a written spec is a first-class artefact and implementation must track it closely.
rules: Write the specification before code and treat it as the source of truth.
Make requirements unambiguous, testable, and free of implementation detail.
Update the spec in the same change as the code it describes.
Trace each implemented behaviour back to a spec clause.

patterns.name: No prescribed test methodology
patterns.description: Tests are still written and run, but they do not drive the order of development.
patterns.whenToUse: When the team explicitly opts out of a test-first methodology, or for throwaway prototypes.
rules: Tests are still required before claiming a task complete.
Do not describe the workflow as TDD/BDD/ATDD/SDD when this option is selected.
Add a regression test for every bug fix.

patterns.name: Factory / Factory Method
patterns.description: Delegate object creation to a method or type so callers depend on an abstraction rather than a concrete constructor.
patterns.whenToUse: When creation logic is conditional, needs configuration, or must be swapped (platform variants, test doubles).
rules: Return interfaces or base types, not concrete classes.
Keep creation logic in one place; do not scatter new calls across the codebase.
Do not let the factory become a god object; split by product family.

patterns.name: Abstract Factory
patterns.description: Create families of related objects through a single interface without naming their concrete classes.
patterns.whenToUse: When the system must be independent of how its products are created and needs consistent product families (theme, platform).
rules: Define one factory interface per product family.
Never reference concrete product classes outside the factory implementations.
Prefer a plain Factory unless multiple related products vary together.

patterns.name: Builder
patterns.description: Construct complex objects step by step, separating construction from representation.
patterns.whenToUse: When an object has many optional parts or a construction sequence that should read clearly.
rules: Expose a fluent, order-independent API where possible.
Return the built object only from a terminal Build() call.
Validate required parts before building.

patterns.name: Prototype
patterns.description: Create new objects by cloning an existing instance instead of constructing from scratch.
patterns.whenToUse: When creation is expensive or configuration is easier to copy than to specify.
rules: Make cloning explicit and deep-copy mutable state to avoid aliasing bugs.
Do not use Prototype when constructors are cheap and configuration is simple.

patterns.name: Singleton
patterns.description: Guarantee a single instance of a type and provide a global access point.
patterns.whenToUse: Only for genuinely global, self-managing services where a single instance is a hard requirement.
rules: Prefer dependency injection over the global access point; inject the instance instead of calling Instance.
Make the instance thread-safe, and lazy only if construction is expensive.
Never use Singleton to pass data between systems; that is a design smell.
Avoid mutable global state; keep the singleton stateless or explicitly synchronised.
patterns.notes: Frequently abused; require an explicit justification before generating one.

patterns.name: Object Pool
patterns.description: Reuse a fixed set of pre-allocated objects instead of allocating and freeing them repeatedly.
patterns.whenToUse: When allocation is frequent and costly (projectiles, particles, enemies) or GC spikes are unacceptable.
rules: Reset object state on release and on acquire.
Return objects to the pool on every path so they are never leaked.
Cap the pool size and define behaviour when exhausted (grow, block, or recycle oldest).
Do not pool cheap, short-lived objects; measure first.

patterns.name: Command
patterns.description: Encapsulate a request as an object so it can be queued, logged, undone, or executed by a different component.
patterns.whenToUse: When you need undo/redo, input remapping, queued actions, or to decouple invokers from receivers.
rules: Give each command a single, well-named Execute (and Undo where needed) operation.
Commands must be self-contained; do not reach into global state.
Keep presentation logic out of commands.

patterns.name: State Machine
patterns.description: Model an object's behaviour as a finite set of states with explicit transitions.
patterns.whenToUse: When behaviour changes with mode and transitions are non-trivial (AI, UI flow, game flow).
rules: Define states and transitions explicitly; do not scatter mode flags through the code.
Keep entry and exit actions in one place per state.
Reject invalid transitions and log them; never ignore silently.
Keep state classes free of unrelated responsibilities.

patterns.name: Strategy
patterns.description: Define a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface and select one at runtime.
patterns.whenToUse: When behaviour varies independently of the context and you want to avoid large conditionals.
rules: Program to the strategy interface; the context must not branch on concrete strategies.
Keep strategies stateless where possible.
Select the strategy through a Factory or DI, not a switch in the context.

patterns.name: Template Method
patterns.description: Define an algorithm skeleton in a base class and let subclasses override specific steps.
patterns.whenToUse: When several algorithms share an identical structure but differ in a few steps.
rules: Keep the skeleton non-overridable; expose only the intended hook steps.
Prefer composition over inheritance when the hierarchy would deepen.

patterns.name: Visitor
patterns.description: Add operations to an object structure without changing the element classes.
patterns.whenToUse: When a stable set of element types needs many unrelated operations.
rules: Keep the element hierarchy stable; a new element type requires updating every visitor.
Do not use Visitor when double dispatch is not actually needed.

patterns.name: Observer
patterns.description: Let subjects notify a dynamic list of subscribers when their state changes.
patterns.whenToUse: When one-to-many change notification is needed and publishers should not know their subscribers.
rules: Always unsubscribe on teardown to prevent leaks and callbacks into destroyed objects.
Do not assume notification order.
Keep handlers small and scoped to their side effects.

patterns.name: Event Bus / Event Channel
patterns.description: A shared publish/subscribe hub that decouples emitters from listeners across the application.
patterns.whenToUse: When many unrelated systems must react to the same events without holding direct references.
rules: Use typed event types; never pass untyped payloads.
Document each event's meaning, publisher, and expected subscribers.
Unsubscribe on teardown; the bus must not keep dead listeners alive.
Do not use the bus for request/response or ordered command flow.

patterns.name: Mediator
patterns.description: Centralise complex communication between colleagues so they do not reference each other directly.
patterns.whenToUse: When many-to-many interactions would otherwise create a tangled dependency graph.
rules: Keep the mediator free of business logic; it only coordinates.
Do not let the mediator become a god object; split by interaction domain.

patterns.name: Dependency Injection (DI)
patterns.description: Supply a component's dependencies from the outside rather than letting it construct or locate them.
patterns.whenToUse: Almost always; it makes code testable and explicit about its dependencies.
rules: Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.
Inject through constructors; avoid service location and static access.
Keep the composition root at the application edge.
Do not inject the container itself.

patterns.name: Service Locator
patterns.description: A global registry that resolves dependencies on demand from inside a component.
patterns.whenToUse: Only as a last resort for legacy code or engine constraints where DI is impossible.
rules: Prefer constructor injection; do not introduce a new Service Locator.
If one already exists, hide it behind explicit dependencies at the boundary.
Never call the locator from deep within domain logic.
patterns.notes: Widely considered an anti-pattern; treat existing usage as a migration target.

patterns.name: Facade
patterns.description: Provide a simplified interface to a complex subsystem.
patterns.whenToUse: When callers should not know about many collaborating classes.
rules: The facade must not add business rules; it only simplifies access.
Do not let the facade expose the entire subsystem.

patterns.name: Adapter
patterns.description: Convert one interface into another that the client expects.
patterns.whenToUse: When integrating third-party or legacy APIs you do not control.
rules: Keep the adapter thin: translate calls and data only.
Do not leak the adapted type's interface to clients.

patterns.name: Decorator
patterns.description: Attach additional behaviour to an object dynamically by wrapping it.
patterns.whenToUse: When responsibilities should be combinable at runtime without a subclass explosion.
rules: Keep each decorator focused on one added responsibility.
Preserve the wrapped interface exactly.

patterns.name: Composite
patterns.description: Treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly through a tree structure.
patterns.whenToUse: When part-whole hierarchies are needed (UI trees, scene graphs, ability trees).
rules: Leaf and composite must share the same interface.
Guard against cycles and unbounded depth.

patterns.name: Proxy
patterns.description: Provide a surrogate that controls access to another object.
patterns.whenToUse: When you need lazy loading, access control, caching, or remote indirection.
rules: The proxy and the real subject must be interchangeable.
Do not put business logic in the proxy.

patterns.name: Entity-Component-System (ECS)
patterns.description: Model state as data components on entities and behaviour as systems that process them, favouring composition over inheritance.
patterns.whenToUse: When performance and data locality matter and there are many similar objects with varied combinations of behaviour.
rules: Keep components as plain data with no logic.
Systems own all behaviour and iterate over component queries.
Prefer composition; do not reintroduce deep inheritance.

patterns.name: Model-View-Controller (MVC)
patterns.description: Separate domain state (Model), presentation (View), and input/coordination (Controller).
patterns.whenToUse: When UI and domain logic must be separated and input handling is non-trivial.
rules: The Model must not reference the View.
Keep the Controller thin: coordinate, do not compute domain rules.
Give each piece of state a single clear owner.

patterns.name: Model-View-Presenter (MVP)
patterns.description: A presenter mediates between a passive view and the model, driving all view updates explicitly.
patterns.whenToUse: When you want highly testable presentation logic and a passive view.
rules: The View exposes an interface and contains no logic.
The Presenter must not reference concrete view types.
Test the Presenter without a UI.

patterns.name: Model-View-ViewModel (MVVM)
patterns.description: A view model exposes observable state and commands that the view binds to declaratively.
patterns.whenToUse: When the UI framework supports data binding and you want two-way binding with testable view models.
rules: The ViewModel must not reference the View.
Expose state through observables and actions through commands.
Keep the ViewModel free of framework-specific view code.

patterns.name: Repository
patterns.description: Mediate between the domain and data-mapping layers using a collection-like interface.
patterns.whenToUse: When domain code should be independent of persistence details.
rules: Return domain objects, never raw storage records or queries.
Keep query logic behind the repository interface.
Do not leak an ORM or session abstraction through the interface.

patterns.name: Unit of Work
patterns.description: Track changes during a business transaction and commit them as one unit.
patterns.whenToUse: When several repositories must change atomically.
rules: Commit once per logical transaction.
Do not share a unit of work across unrelated transactions or threads.

patterns.name: Producer-Consumer
patterns.description: Decouple producers and consumers through a shared, bounded queue.
patterns.whenToUse: When work arrives faster than it can be processed or must be processed on another thread.
rules: Always bound the queue and define back-pressure behaviour.
Make the queue thread-safe; never share mutable state without synchronisation.
Handle shutdown by draining or cancelling deterministically.

patterns.name: Actor
patterns.description: Isolate state inside an actor that processes messages one at a time, communicating only by messages.
patterns.whenToUse: When concurrency must be safe by construction across many independent units of state.
rules: Never access an actor's state from outside; send messages instead.
Process one message at a time per actor; do not block the actor loop.
Design for message ordering and idempotency.
